The Global Antiauthoritarian Wave Is an Illusion

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, LARRY M.
  • Sources indicate that in 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy.
  • But that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, LARRY M. BARTELS is University Distinguished Professor of Political Science and Law and May Werthan Shayne Chair of Public Policy and Social Science at Vanderbilt University.

Democracy Can’t Be Saved at the Ballot Box.

Sources indicate that in 2022, many observers celebrated the results of the United States’ midterm elections as a victory for democracy. The Republican Party underperformed at the ballot box, and some of the candidates most outspoken in support of former President Donald Trump’s historic effort to overturn the 2020 election outcome were among the casualties. President Joe Biden concluded that the American people “have proven once again that democracy is who we are.” Reporters for The New York Times concurred, writing that the midterm outcome demonstrated “the resilience of the country’s democracy” as the electorate rejected “openly extremist Republican candidates.”.

But that rosy interpretation was more the result of wishful thinking than careful analysis. Most of the Republicans who lost were simply bad, inexperienced candidates. In fact, Republican members of Congress who had flouted the democratic process by voting to decertify electoral votes on January 6, 2021, suffered no discernible penalty at the polls, while the minority who had stood up for the rule of law faced stiff backlash from their party’s establishment and from primary voters. And, of course, two years later, Trump stormed back into the White House.

Sources indicate that in this year’s midterms, Trump’s party took another, even bigger beating. And again, there has been a rush to celebrate the result as a triumph for democratic values. NPR reported that “one of the substantial, clear winners of the midterms is American democracy itself.” Amanda Taub, an international affairs columnist at The Fresh York Times, upped the ante, writing that “An anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world.” Just as in 2022, however, there is reason to fear that this optimistic account seriously misconstrues what happened at the polls on November 3 and what the result means for the future. History highlights that voters in the United States, as in other democracies, are much more focused on the competence of their political leaders and their own well-being than on adherence to democratic procedures. To imagine that they have suddenly become guardians of democratic norms is to misunderstand the electorate’s role in the democratic process—and to underestimate the chronic susceptibility of the American political system to democratic backsliding.

It is natural to “feel pride,” as the New York Times editorial board put it, in the notion that ordinary citizens “stood up” for democratic principles at the ballot box. Democracy is the United States’ civil religion, and the voice of the people is the closest thing Americans have to the voice of God. But as the British jurist and historian Henry Sumner Maine observed in 1885, the oracle of democracy is often “not as intelligible as might be desired.” Electoral behavior is complex, and interpretations of election outcomes constructed in the hours and days after a vote often turn out to be far off the mark. Voters in democracies are less ideological than analysts generally assume. They are also less committed to abstract democratic norms than high-minded observers might hope. In a 2020 study, the Yale political scientists Matthew Graham and Milan Svolik used survey experiments to test the impact of democratic norm violations on Americans’ support for hypothetical candidates. They concluded that “only a small fraction of Americans prioritize democratic principles in their electoral choices when doing so goes against their partisan identification or favorite policies.” In 2022, real voters demonstrated the same point with their willingness to support Republican members of Congress who had participated in Trump’s bogus “stop the steal” effort.

This year, the exit polls run by a consortium of American news organizations provided superficial support for the notion that the midterm “blue wave” was an explicit rejection of Trump’s continuing assault on democratic norms. These surveys asked voters which of six challenges was the most crucial facing the country. A third of respondents chose “the state of democracy,” and an overwhelming proportion of those who did, 79 percent, voted for Democratic congressional candidates. Taken at face value, these data suggest that more than a quarter of the electorate voted Democratic because they opposed Trump’s efforts to subvert American democracy.

It has been revealed that alas, people’s explanations for their own behavior are often misleading. Responses to list choices of this sort are particularly sensitive to the specific options presented and their favorable or unfavorable connotations. Given the choice, most people would probably prefer to attribute their votes to principled support for democracy than to pique at the price of gas. But when a separate YouGov poll conducted just after the vote asked an open-ended version of the same question, only five percent of voters spontaneously cited government corruption or the undermining of democracy as the most notable factor motivating their choice.

A closer look at the exit poll data offers additional grounds for skepticism regarding the importance of democratic principles for the 2026 midterm outcome. The largest swing away from the Republican Party, more than 30 points, was among young voters—who are generally much less supportive of democracy than other age cohorts. (A 2025 Kettering Foundation survey, for instance, found that although 89 percent of Silent Generation respondents agreed with the proposition that “democracy is the best form of government,” only 54 percent of Gen Z respondents did.) To suppose that young people are now the vanguard of a sudden urge to defend democracy is implausible.

Finally, a comparison between the 2026 and 2024 exit polls is telling. In 2022, well before the depredations of Trump’s second term, voters were presented a similar list choice of concerns that “mattered most in deciding how you voted for president.” A similar share of voters cited “the state of democracy” that year as did this year, and a similar overwhelming majority of them reported voting for Kamala Harris. The key difference between the two elections was not in the importance that voters assigned to democratic principles but in the impact of economic grievances. In 2024, 32 percent of exit poll respondents noted the economy mattered most for their vote, and 81 percent of those respondents reported voting for Trump. In 2026, 39 percent said that the economy was the most important issue facing the country—and most of them voted for Democrats.

What about the notion that “an anti-authoritarian wave appears to be crashing over elections around the world”? As with many “waves” identified by political analysts, this antiauthoritarian trend mostly amounts to a short list of cases in which autocrats (or would-be autocrats) lost elections. Taub, the New York Times commentator, pointed to Brazil, Hungary, and Serbia, along with the U.S. midterm elections, as evidence for a wave. But it is a stretch to see antiauthoritarian sentiment as the common thread explaining these outcomes.

In Brazil in October, the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (known as Lula), defeated Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of his right-wing populist predecessor, by less than four percentage points. The result was unremarkable, except for the fact that Bolsonaro had led Lula in the first round of voting. The most salient event separating the two votes was a televised debate in which Bolsonaro seemed to mock Lula for having lost a finger in a factory accident. “I was a minor and working at night,” Lula responded, “because either I worked or I did not eat. I will not accept a posh guy calling me ‘nine-fingers.’ ” It was a dramatic moment, but hardly a test of Brazilian voters’ commitment to democracy.

The April election in Hungary provides a clearer parallel with the U.S. midterm race. Viktor Orban’s Fidesz party was defeated after 16 years of autocratic rule—but Hungarians’ attitudes toward democracy likely played a smaller role in both Orban’s rise and his fall than many observers imagine. His triumph in 2010 was widely but erroneously portrayed as part of a global populist wave. In fact, data from the European Social Survey (ESS) show that his supporters were not more distrustful of politicians, more dissatisfied with democracy, more opposed to immigration or the EU, or more eager for order and tradition than other Hungarian voters. What they were, mostly, was fed up with their incumbent government.

In a recent development, orban used his sweeping election victory as a pretext to substantially erode Hungarian democracy, pressuring judges and the press and fiddling with election rules to entrench Fidesz’s dominance. Those moves no doubt contributed to his long tenure in office. But the more important factor was that, from 2009 to 2019, a series of ESS surveys recorded substantial increases in ordinary Hungarians’ satisfaction with their economy, their government, their lives as a whole, and, ironically, even “the way democracy works in Hungary.” When that sense of well-being faded, Orban’s autocratic machinations proved unable to protect him. As the Christian Science Monitor reporter Mark Sappenfield put it, “The story of his political demise is, in the end, not so different from countless democratic elections everywhere. The economy stagnated, highlighting levels of corruption that became intolerable to voters, who then lost trust in Mr. Orbán’s ability to guide them to better lives.”.

Industry observers note that much the same could be said of Trump in 2026. One of the oldest and best-supported generalizations in political science is the law of the pendulum. It asserts that the political costs of governing—stemming from, for example, ideological overreach, complacency, scandals, or economic shocks—tend to erode support for incumbent political leaders and their parties, resulting in the restoration of competitive balance and periodic alteration of parties in power. Of course, these political costs do not accumulate with anything like the uniformity implied by the image of a pendulum swinging consistently from left to right and back again. Some governments are beset by problems and succumb in short order, while others face smoother seas and survive—for a time. But no democratic government lasts forever.

Sources indicate that when incumbents use state resources—sometimes including legal and physical intimidation—to entrench themselves in power, it may feel like the law of the pendulum has been suspended. Nonetheless, even the most dominant political machines succumb eventually to hard times, economic and social change, internal divisions, and mounting pressure from those excluded from power. As the Vanderbilt political scientist Jessica Trounstine noted in a 2008 study of the rise and fall of political “bosses” in U.S. cities, the result may be chaotic: “In many cases the fall of monopolies set in motion periods of intense factionalism during which gridlock was common.” Turnover may result in protracted turmoil or in the emergence of a new machine, perhaps under the banner of reform. The fall of a strongman or boss does not automatically produce a well-functioning democratic system.

If characterizing the midterm elections as a triumph for democratic norms misconstrues why voters made their choices, it also risks misrepresenting what comes next. The Newly introduced York Times editorial board envisioned quick progress to halt democratic backsliding: “The outcome creates a crucial check on Mr. Trump’s autocratic behavior. . . . The country already feels changed, and it will in fact be changed in January.”.

Changed, certainly; but the president and his allies are not going anywhere, and they are far from powerless. A glance around the world provides examples of the intense factionalism and gridlock that may be in store for the United States during the next two years. In Poland, an autocratic government fell in 2023 after eight years in power. But the holdover president, Karol Nawrocki, has battled Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s institutional reform efforts. Tusk’s attempt to remake the constitutional court—packed with friends of the former regime—precipitated a constitutional crisis pitting the prime minister and the EU against the president and mobs of right-wing protesters. Tusk’s election was just one step in what will be a long struggle to restore Poland’s liberal democracy.

In a recent development, the American president is much more powerful than Poland’s, providing much more scope for bitter political conflict over policies and democratic procedures. In one election-night interview, Trump claimed that he would “look forward to working with” the victorious Democrats. But earlier in the day, to CBS News’s Robert Costa, he noted his victory in the Supreme Court case Trump v. Slaughter (which upheld his right to fire a Federal Trade Commission member) and claimed that “the Slaughter case gives the president tremendous powers that it never had before.” Another person Costa described as “close to the president” told him that “while Democrats may win” the election, the president would “keep the power to do almost everything he wants.” The post-election appointment of Stephen Miller as Trump’s chief of staff does not bode well for cooperation.

Sources indicate that of course, Democrats hope to win back the White House in 2028. But even if they do, it would be naive to expect Trump’s legacy of democratic backsliding to be erased. He has done substantial, durable harm to the federal government and the American political system. Some of his most egregious procedural and policy changes will be rolled back, but only by diverting attention and political capital from upcoming priorities. Others will be harder to undo. Millions of years’ worth of governing experience cast aside in Elon Musk’s ham-handed purge of the civil service will not be restored with the stroke of a pen. The massive expansion of the Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency, its extensive network of detention facilities, and its culture—which the legal scholar L. Ali Khan described as “performative cruelty”—will not be swiftly or easily dismantled. The Supreme Court will not revert to the ideological mainstream any time soon.

Perhaps the most significant damage of the Trump era has been to long-standing, informal democratic norms that supposedly constrained the behavior of political leaders. Observers who expected Trump to pay a stiff political price for his abusive rhetoric, incessant lying, self-dealing, and disdain for court rulings, Congress, foreign allies, and the electoral process have learned that, as the University of Denver political scientist Seth Masket put it, “a lot of the things we think voters just won’t tolerate turn out to be tolerable to them.” That lesson, once learned, is very hard to unlearn. If future political leaders refrain from these behaviors, it will be because they want to, not because they think they have to.

Trump’s trashing of political norms accelerated a process that was already underway before he turned his sights on the White House. In 2012, the veteran political analysts Thomas Mann and Norman Ornstein argued that hyperpartisanship was eroding the compromise and self-restraint necessary to facilitate power sharing in the United States’ peculiarly decentralized national government. The logic of partisan tit for tat has encouraged each party to respond to the other’s norm violations by pushing even more aggressively to weaponize the filibuster, bypass Congress with executive orders, and gerrymander congressional district boundaries. Each successful norm violation has encouraged further probing of legal and political redlines.

In a recent development, hyperpartisanship will not disappear when Trump departs the political scene; he is its consequence more than its cause. Most vital, the passion that has fueled the Make America Great Again movement will not vanish. Millions of Americans still see the waves of social change that have washed over the United States since the 1960s as a cultural disaster, and the looming prospect of a majority-minority country as a threat to be battled, by undemocratic means if necessary. They will find upcoming champions.

A survey commissioned by NPR and PBS to mark the United States’ 250th birthday found that 82 percent of Americans agreed that “the challenges that divide the nation” constitute “a serious threat to the future of our democracy.” If that seems alarmist, it is worth noting that 37 percent of the same respondents in the same survey—and 58 percent of those under the age of 30—agreed that “Americans may have to resort to violence in order to get the country back on track.” When people view political conflict in existential terms, they are unlikely to feel constrained by high-minded democratic theory.

Tech Report: Significant Tech Has Undermined Democracy. Here’s How to Reverse the Trend.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • These trends have come alongside a corresponding rise in attempts to explain this phenomenon, ranging from feckless leadership and rising inequality to globalization and economic shocks.
  • It is now common to lament a crisis in the system of democracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

In a recent development, it is now common to lament a crisis in the system of democracy. Confidence in public institutions has declined, experts are dismissed, and politics is becoming a contest over not only values and interests but reality itself.

These trends have come alongside a corresponding rise in attempts to explain this phenomenon, ranging from feckless leadership and rising inequality to globalization and economic shocks. While those are all factors, a more compelling explanation could lie in how the digital revolution has undermined trust in facts, governments, and democracy itself.

It is now common to lament a crisis in the system of democracy. Confidence in public institutions has declined, experts are dismissed, and politics is becoming a contest over not only values and interests but reality itself.

Recent findings suggest that these trends have come alongside a corresponding rise in attempts to explain this phenomenon, ranging from feckless leadership and rising inequality to globalization and economic shocks. While those are all factors, a more compelling explanation could lie in how the digital revolution has undermined trust in facts, governments, and democracy itself.

To be clear, falsehoods and disinformation are not fresh. Manipulating information has long been a tool of statecraft. The ancient Indian political treatise, the Arthashastra, advised rulers to spread rumors to control public opinion. But while modern media has vastly expanded the scale, scope, and reach of information, it has also turbocharged the dissemination of propaganda and misinformation.

This degradation of informational systems is precipitating a crisis of legitimacy in the core institutions of democracies. Meanwhile, there is a growing mismatch between inherited democratic institutions and our newly introduced social realities. In some countries, the central problem is the decay of once-strong mass intermediaries such as political parties, unions, a free press, and civic organizations. In others, mass intermediaries never achieved the authority imagined in the classic democratic model. In others, the state itself remains too uneven or predatory to serve as a reliable object of trust. But in all cases, democracies face a similar problem: how to make collective self-government credible when citizens no longer accept inherited intermediaries as authoritative or trustworthy.

What is the solution? There is no easy answer, but a path to restoring faith in democracy can only begin by making the democratic process more observable, relational, and capable. And this process must take place first at the local level, building from the bottom up—just as democracy was designed to do.

In a recent development, audience members hold up their phones during fashion week in Sao Paulo on Oct. 28, 2018. Mauricio Santana/Getty Images.

Trust—among citizens and between citizens and their governments—is the bedrock of democracy. Trust represents a pact between the trustor—the party extending the trust—and the trustee, or the party being trusted. Such a transaction requires a degree of vulnerability on the part of the trustor. Trust is a psychological condition that allows the trustor to set aside a purely rational calculus and make a leap of faith toward positive expectations about the trustee.

We can distinguish between two types of trust: cognition-based and affect-based. The former is an evidence-driven process by which individuals use updated information to judge the reliability, character, and ability of the trustee. Affect-based trust, in contrast, underpins social relationships and is based on emotions of care and concern for others.

In politics, cognitive trust is based on calculated assessments of the competence of politicians and governments based on tangible metrics such as economic growth, inflation, and crime. To feel this form of trust, voters need to have access to information they find reliable and the bandwidth to process it. This is decreasingly the case.

What is left is affective trust. This is driven by emotional bonds and shared identities and values. Affective judgments lead citizens to base their voting decisions on the person rather than the policies, on feelings rather than facts. This matters because new media—especially social media—is particularly adept at amplifying emotionally charged discourse. Such narratives are stickier than verifiable facts, and their participatory nature converts audiences from passive consumers to active co-authors churning out their own alternative narratives. These dynamics become even more febrile in an era of uncertainty. The result is emotionally driven discourse increasingly shaping public opinion, with facts becoming collateral damage.

Silicon Valley is becoming an instrument of U.S. coercion, and that’s a danger to each and every country.

Recent findings suggest that voters repose both cognition-based and affect-based trust in politicians and the state. But to the extent the information environment deteriorates—what Steve Bannon, U.S. President Donald Trump’s former advisor, once referred to as “flooding the zone”—the attention economy constricts cognitive bandwidth. The result, as Herbert Simon famously noted, is a “poverty of attention.” The arc of trust then bends toward affective trust. Emotional attachments to personalities acquire greater salience. This may explain, at least partly, the current wave of populism.

According to recent reports, in 2023, 44 percent of citizens surveyed by the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development reported no or low trust in their governments. In 2025, in the United States, trust in government fell to near its lowest recorded level, with just 17 percent of Americans saying they trusted the federal government to do what is right.

In a recent development, democracy depends on trust at scale. A resident of New Jersey will rarely meet an Alaskan. In the modern era, their sense of collective fate is bound together by shared sources of authority, such as official documents, and means of disseminating commonly trusted information, such as news broadcasts. If achieving broad impersonal trust was one of the unsung accomplishments of the modern state, this was made possible by mass institutions such as unions, parties, and a reliable media ecosystem.

According to recent reports, both mass institutions and impersonal trust are deteriorating. Given the structure of the current information environment, these are unlikely to be revived. As mass trust has fragmented, particularized trust—in personalities, partisan leaders, or online communities—seems to be on the rise. There is no source of certification that is accepted at scale.

Misinformation is hard to defeat with truth alone; it requires truth to be tethered to a trusted authority transmitting the message. As trust has fragmented, attacking misinformation has become more complicated, requiring more than mere correction. When societies no longer trust a single common referee, it is hard to achieve broad acceptance of the contest they adjudicate.

It has been revealed that A voter exits a booth at a polling station in Lancaster, Latest Hampshire, on Nov. 5, 2024.Joseph Prezioso/AFP via Getty Images.

Where do we go from here? We believe that rebuilding citizens’ trust in their governments will increasingly require the lived experience of national polities to occur at smaller scales where citizens can see public purpose enacted. Such public policy would be made not only in legislatures and ministries but also in the everyday discretion of frontline workers.

This is one reason that street-level bureaucracy matters so much. Citizens rarely encounter a national government. Instead, their primary encounters are with the local state—a teacher, a social worker, a police officer, a sanitation worker, a building inspector, a nurse, a benefits caseworker, a public meeting, a pothole crew, a school board, or a public transport employee. These encounters represent democracy’s front line. They are the key to a more capable state, which in turn boosts the state’s legitimacy and builds trust.

Sources indicate that smaller administrative units are more conducive for building trust because they can collectively draw on tacit knowledge and shared networks, repeat interactions, and direct observation. Engagement at this local level with the broader state can build relational state capacity—reciprocal relationships where both parties feel seen and understood by the other. Local units are primary sites of trust formation, handling decisions that depend heavily on contextual knowledge and observable accountability. Regional or national government can support the local, but in this model, trust ultimately flows up from the local rather than down from a pinnacle source, be that a Walter Cronkite, the United Nations, or a national leader.

In a recent development, three principles are fundamental to creating this upcoming reality. First, democracy must become more observable. Presently, citizens are asked to trust many things they cannot personally experience, such as central bank decisions, vaccine approvals, or election integrity. Some of this is unavoidable. A meeting to set a central bank’s interest rate will inevitably be an elite club. But many of these things don’t need to be opaque. Election infrastructure is needs greater transparency, incorporating community at the local level; many more opportunities for sustained citizen interaction, personal observation, and collective public judgment can and should be found. Citizens must be able to connect what they observe to public purpose. More quotidian, regular interaction with the state—not more online portals or structured public hearings—will help democracies build trust. Public work should be organized so that its progress, purpose, and challenges are intelligible to everyday citizens.

Second, democracy must become more relational. Trust will not emerge from public information messaging, but rather from repeated interactions where people can upgrade their beliefs about one another. Mutual respect is key to interactions that build trust and expand the definition of community. Citizens do not need more exposure to opposing views; they need structured settings in which disagreement is part of a collective effort to constructively govern. Schools, juries, unions, and civic organizations show us the potential of these types of forums. Citizens must have the opportunity to assess whether officials listen, keep commitments, and exercise judgment with care. Officials, in turn, need to gain knowledge about citizens that administrative categories alone cannot supply. Building local trust requires rethinking how we create space for relationship building and empowerment of front-line workers. It also requires institutions that provide attentive treatment even to those who arrive without influence or connections.

Third, democracy must become more capable. The administrative state is the front door of democracy; it cannot be an afterthought. Simply put, the state must be able to deliver on its promises. Capability is not merely technical prowess, however. Complex collective problems often require multiple centers of decision-making, local knowledge, monitoring, and rule adaptation, as well as coproduction between the state and society. Front-line workers need not only have skills but also authority, organizational support, and flexibility for the state to become more capable.

It has been revealed that focusing on local communities can have a surprising international effect. By Gordon Brown.

It is tempting to respond to malfeasance and unequal treatment with layers of compliance such as rules, audits, targets, and procedural safeguards. Some are necessary. But when we set things up so bad that actions can never happen again, as contrite managers often say, we consign ourselves to a suboptimal, constrained state. Too much regulation makes public servants less able to solve problems or act in ways that citizens recognize as responsive. A state that exercises judgment capriciously and arbitrarily will not earn citizens’ trust, but neither will a state that cannot exercise judgment at all.

According to recent reports, these principles are meant to complement rather than substitute for national and transnational units of government. The national unit cannot be a mere composite of local experience. States will need to adapt to the changing architecture of trust, which will require rethinking accountability. A focus on thin metrics will need to be replaced with a broader collective justification. That channel of accountability should, whenever possible, run from those engaging with citizens to those citizens themselves, rather than up the hierarchy to supervisors in a distant office. National institutions can rebuild trust through more reliable local encounters that their resources and coordination make possible.

Industry observers note that however, these principles will have to confront the elephant in the room—technology. In recent years, new technologies, first digital and now artificial intelligence, have been fanning the fires of mistrust. National governments will especially need to play an active role in facilitating robust safety standards for new technologies. It will be exceedingly difficult to rebuild trust without first strengthening faith in these technologies themselves. Historically, technology standards have been built by professionals within the sector—not through government regulation—recognizing that guardrails are fundamental to building trust and thereby the long-term prospects of the technology. After the internet was established, the refusal of the tech giants to build strong universal safety standards sowed the very seeds of mistrust that are now coming back to haunt them. If this occurs with artificial intelligence, a much more consequential technology, the fallout will be even more dire.

Sources indicate that youth gather at a community center in downtown Rio de Janeiro in October 2007. Tom Stoddart/Getty Images.

Industry observers note that democracy first flourished in settings where citizens could assemble face to face. Mass institutions and new technologies allowed democracy to scale. One consequence was that the primacy of the local as the locus of trust, and ultimately where democracy thrived, withered. More recently, the deluge of information has also vastly increased the speed and scope of misinformation. But going forward, information will be increasingly produced—and consumed—by machines. The ructions from this shift will profoundly change the informational landscape and, with it, the cognitive foundations of democracy.

Rebuilding and nourishing the local roots of democracy should become an urgent imperative for societies, not simply in a geographically proximate sense, but incorporating any forum where members come to accept and trust one another. For governments, the lesson is not to control or dictate to these communities, but to scaffold and connect them. This, in turn, requires making the state more capable, more relational, and more observable. Governments will also have to coordinate to build stronger safety standards for the technologies that are enmeshed in the burgeoning labyrinths of mistrust.

It has been revealed that democracy will only be rebuilt if the corrosiveness of mistrust is reversed. We must accept what we cannot change—that the structure of information has drastically changed, and there will be no innovation that yields a rebirth of mass, impersonal democracy. The future of democratic trust depends not on our screens but on our neighborhoods. If we can no longer trust from the top down, then we must rebuild it from the bottom up.

Dan Honig is an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McCourt School of Public Policy and University College London’s department of political science.

Devesh Kapur is the Starr Foundation professor of South Asian studies at the School of Advanced International Studies at Johns Hopkins University.

Industry observers note that dr. Joel Brown, a communication expert, shares how replacing one common phrase and asking a simple question can help defuse disagreements and keep holiday gatherings civil.

As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, states swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.

In a recent development, "‘But’ shows disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation.".

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he said. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions.".

Dr. Joel Brown states the holiday dinner table can quickly become a source of tension when family members disagree, but choosing the right words can make all the difference in preventing heated exchanges. (iStock).

If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that.".

The question, he says, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate.

He also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he mentioned, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion.

According to recent reports, "If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown said. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective.".

Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together.

Sources indicate that for personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss.

According to recent reports, additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown noted people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction.

He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position.

Industry News: How Europe Comes Apart

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MUJTABA RAHMAN is Managing Director for Europe at Eurasia Group.
  • The Four Elections That Could Seal the Continent’s Fate.
  • Recent findings suggest that the European Union is entering a period of political instability that could threaten its future—not through its formal dissolution, but through the gradual erosion of its capacity to act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MUJTABA RAHMAN is Managing Director for Europe at Eurasia Group.

The Four Elections That Could Seal the Continent’s Fate.

Recent findings suggest that the European Union is entering a period of political instability that could threaten its future—not through its formal dissolution, but through the gradual erosion of its capacity to act. In recent months, Europe has been engulfed in protests driven by a common crisis of affordability, deteriorating public services, and declining confidence in governments’ ability to improve living standards, especially for young people.

The protests that have swept across France, Germany, Italy, and Spain are not a single, coordinated European movement, but they reflect underlying problems that are increasingly common to a growing number of EU countries: a mounting perception that governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services, and economic security. This widening gap between the public’s expectations and the economic and fiscal reality confronting many EU countries is only likely to grow over time. It could prompt Spanish voters to unseat Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez this weekend and usher in a right-wing government that includes the far-right party Vox. And it sets up 2027 to be a strikingly consequential year, as nine elections across the EU could completely remake the continent’s complexion.

Four of those elections, in France, Germany, Italy, and Poland, will be particularly important. In each of them, far-right populist forces could rise to the fore and turn their countries against greater EU integration, support for Ukraine, and collective European security. But dangers remain even if the far right does not win outright at the polls. A plethora of electoral outcomes could still see fresh governments pull away from Brussels and vitiate attempts to strengthen European autonomy and defense. Instead of a bang, the European project could die with a whimper.

It has been revealed that the most consequential race will be in France. A series of domestic and international developments, along with a volatile national mood, have combined to make Marine Le Pen the front-runner to win the April 2027 election and become France’s first far-right president since the dissolution of the Vichy regime in 1944.

It has been revealed that in October, riots and looting marred a series of mostly peaceful protests against high prices and deteriorating schools in a score of French cities. Those images—along with the diffuse sense of a country in paralysis—have shredded whatever remained of the domestic credibility of President Emmanuel Macron and his minority centrist coalition. Édouard Philippe, the strongest centrist contender to succeed Macron, has been tarnished by association. The first poll since the riots, conducted by IFOP for Le Figaro, showed Le Pen’s support among potential voters rising to 36 percent, her highest level to date, while support for Philippe fell three points from a month earlier to 15 percent.

In a recent development, philippe and the other centrist challenger, Gabriel Attal, another Macron-era prime minister, were already losing support because of high energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Both candidates remain stuck between seven percent and 15 percent in the polls, and their campaigns have generated little momentum or popular enthusiasm.

It has been revealed that meanwhile, an opportunistic coalition of far-left extremists and young looters from the poor multiracial suburbs of French cities who were responsible for much of the violence in October will hurt the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has been accused by the government of helping incite the unrest. He has certainly failed to condemn the disturbances. But the disorder has not dampened his allure, as support for his candidacy has risen to between 17 and 19 percent in polling, which makes him a credible contender to reach the second-round runoff against Le Pen. Unfortunately for Mélenchon, polls suggest that Le Pen would thump him in the second round, by at least 65 percent to 35 percent.

The election seems very much Le Pen’s to lose. No presidential candidate since the Fifth Republic began in 1958 has held such a commanding first-round lead in opinion polls five months before election day and lost.

Industry observers note that A Le Pen presidency would be nothing short of an earthquake for Europe. It would deliver a death blow to the EU’s ambition of greater “strategic autonomy”: Brussels’ goal of achieving greater political independence from the United States and China, primarily via more European integration. This was a vision espoused by Macron in a speech at the Sorbonne in September 2017, in which he called for a “sovereign, united, and democratic Europe.” Le Pen is committed to unilaterally (and illegally) withholding French contributions to the EU budget; to ending French and EU aid to Ukraine; to restraining all EU spending; to blocking the enlargement of the EU to neighboring countries; and changing the French constitution to enshrine “national” primacy in jobs and welfare, which would effectively destroy the European single market. She may be denied some of these ambitions, but a hostile Paris could very easily stymie any forward movement of the EU.

In a recent development, centrist governments are on the defensive beyond France, as voters across the continent conclude that they do not have the solutions to address their problems. Germany is a case in point. A weak and unpopular chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is finding it difficult to hold off the rise of the far-right, neo-Nazi Alternative for Germany party, known as the AfD, which continues to make sweeping electoral gains across the country.

In a recent development, merz has to steward an economy that is struggling after decades serving as Europe’s industrial core. Although it is true that Germany’s economic outlook in 2026 and 2027 has brightened after almost flat growth in 2025, its recovery is driven exclusively by the government’s debt-financed investment programs. Key industries, including those to do with automobiles, machinery, pharmaceuticals, and chemicals, are still suffering from high energy prices, crumbling infrastructure, and a shrinking workforce.

China’s aggressive trade practices, deliberately aimed at undermining some of Germany’s core sectors, continue to put pressure on German companies. The unwinding of the international trade system also disproportionately hurts Germany’s export-driven economy. So does Europe’s fragmented and undercapitalized banking sector, which provides too little venture capital for German start-ups to scale up quickly. For these reasons, Berlin will have a hard time limiting significant job losses in its industrial sectors in 2027.

Industry observers note that the result will be unemployment and growing electoral disgruntlement that Merz’s government will be poorly placed to address. If anything, the divides between the chancellor’s conservative camp and his coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats, will prevent the government from delivering decisive reforms related to pensions, taxes, health care, the labor market, energy, and climate.

Five state elections in 2027, two of which are in the key states of North Rhine–Westphalia and Lower Saxony, will exacerbate this divide. Merz’s Christian Democrats will be vying for seats with the Social Democrats, keeping the two sides in a permanent competition that could prevent the coalition from governing effectively at the federal level. And that competition will likely be in vain: state election results for both parties will almost certainly be disappointing, leading to growing restiveness and speculation about Merz’s future as chancellor.

In a recent development, these centrifugal forces within the government will collide with the determination of both parties to stay in the coalition and avoid provoking a fresh election. This will result in a largely paralyzed government, discredited centrist politics, and a widening sense of malaise across an already unhappy and disaffected electorate.

Industry observers note that as the center struggles, the AfD on the far right and Die Linke on the hard left will continue to gather national momentum. For the first time, the AfD will almost certainly penetrate deeply into the electorates of Germany’s western industrial strongholds in state elections next year, hollowing out the constituencies of both Christian Democrats and Social Democrats. With its sights on the 2029 federal elections, the AfD will increasingly look like a national contender rather than a protest movement rooted in eastern Germany. Die Linke, for its part, will continue to siphon off votes from left-leaning parties with its platform of economic grievance, disinterest in support for Ukraine, and the highly successful mobilization of young voters around support for Palestinians. The gains of both parties will further splinter state parliaments and make the process of government formation at that level increasingly cumbersome. The resulting state administrations will likely be unstable and doomed to performing poorly, deepening voter disillusionment with party politics and encouraging a greater willingness to experiment with radicalism.

Industry observers note that these electoral pressures in Germany and in France make it likely that the relationship between Berlin and Paris will grow strained. A nationalist-populist president Le Pen would have little interest in sustaining the French-German “engine”—the traditional motor of European integration. Le Pen’s political priority of cutting French payments to the EU would rankle Germany, the largest contributor to the EU budget. And any government in Berlin would be unlikely to accommodate French positions, especially those of a disruptive Le Pen presidency, such as weakening the single market or abandoning Ukraine.

It has been revealed that without convergence between French and German policy, it will be harder for the EU’s other states to build consensus on the economic and security challenges that matter most. This prospect has encouraged European policymakers to look east, toward Poland, and ask what “latest Europe” can do if “old Europe” ceases to drive the EU forward. Yet Warsaw faces its own political troubles, and it will struggle to galvanize the continent if France and Germany fall away.

In a recent development, poland will stage consequential parliamentary elections next year. The vote could bring the overthrow of the current centrist coalition and the creation of a far-right coalition government involving the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, the far-right Confederation Liberty and Independence, and the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).

A coalition formed by all three would mark a significant shift in Poland’s domestic and foreign policy. Such a government would adopt a more confrontational approach toward the EU, particularly on the complications of migration, climate policy, judicial independence, and the next seven-year EU budget. Although PiS remains broadly supportive of NATO and Ukraine, Confederation and especially the KKP have adopted a more critical stance toward Kyiv. Their participation in the government could therefore erode Poland’s support for Ukraine, including its military and financial assistance to its embattled neighbor, and lead to tougher policies regarding Ukrainian refugees, nearly one million of whom remain in Poland after fleeing Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, according to Eurostat.

Significant ideological differences among the three parties, particularly over economic policy, would probably make this far-right coalition unstable. PiS’s preference for social spending and state intervention sits uneasily alongside Confederation’s economically liberal agenda. Moreover, the leader of PiS, Jaroslaw Kaczynski, has repeatedly ruled out cooperation with KKP’s leader, Grzegorz Braun, describing him as “very dangerous” and his party as “completely unserious.” A far-right government could be quite short-lived, if it emerges at all.

In a recent development, an alternative but equally problematic scenario would involve a hung parliament in which neither Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) nor PiS could assemble a governing majority, resulting in a weak minority government or even fresh elections. Fragmentation among smaller parties and disagreements over potential coalition partners could prolong negotiations, particularly if PiS refuses to cooperate with KKP while Tusk’s coalition lacks sufficient support from centrist and left-wing parties. Even if a minority government were formed, its dependence on opposition parties for legislative support could severely constrain policymaking, leaving Poland unable to address its mounting security challenges or play any leadership role in Brussels.

In a recent development, italy, meanwhile, presents a different risk. Unlike France, Germany, or Poland, it presently has a relatively stable government led by a prime minister, Giorgi Meloni, who has reconciled her far-right nationalist origins with a broadly pragmatic approach to European and foreign affairs. Indeed, Meloni has become something of a poster child of far-right moderation, held up as evidence that ultranationalists can become responsible European leaders. But that equilibrium could be upset by the emergence of a newly introduced political force even further to Meloni’s right.

In a recent development, meloni remains the favorite to win next year’s election. But she is threatened by Roberto Vannacci, a former paratrooper and veteran of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars who has rolled out a new party, National Future (FN), that is peeling away right-wing voters from Meloni with a nationalist, populist agenda that is skeptical of NATO and support for Ukraine. His goal is to court Italians aggrieved by Meloni’s compromises with Brussels.

The worst-case scenario would be a right-wing majority in which FN holds the balance of power and chooses to use it. That outcome would require the party to outperform expectations, approaching or exceeding ten percent of the vote—FN is currently polling at 6.5 percent—while Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party slips to around 20 percent or below. The coalition would still govern, but its center of gravity would shift decisively to the right, and Meloni would no longer have a firm grip at the helm.

Recent findings suggest that vannacci would likely not moderate his positions once in government, as Meloni did. Instead, he would maximize his leverage, up to and including threatening to pull out of the coalition and trigger snap elections, to extract concessions regarding Italy’s relations to Europe. His strategy would be deliberately confrontational: squeezing Meloni between the demands of his right-wing base and the constraints imposed by the EU, NATO, and the bond markets. The aim would be less to shape policy than to build his own visibility and lure supporters away from Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. Faced with a direct challenge on her right flank, Meloni would be forced to prioritize her own political survival, pulling the government toward more unorthodox positions.

The effects would be most acute in foreign policy, as Italy moved from the consensual position it has adopted on Ukraine to more active opposition, a major challenge at a time when EU decision-making on Ukraine, defense, and the EU budget depends heavily on unanimity among the EU’s largest members. Italy could transform from a pragmatic, generally constructive player in Brussels into a more disruptive force, blocking or threatening to veto decisions on bilateral and EU-wide support for Ukraine. Alongside a far-right Paris, Rome would also block Ukraine’s path to EU accession. On EU financial matters, Italy would straddle Germany and France, siding with Berlin in opposing any increase in the bloc’s next budget and with Paris in resisting cuts to agriculture and funding for the EU’s poorest regions, narrowing the space for a deal on the EU’s next seven-year budget and certainly curtailing its geopolitical ambitions. Under pressure from Vannacci, Meloni could also be forced to abandon NATO’s target for member states to spend five percent of GDP on their militaries and even forgo her planned incremental increases in military spending.

Industry observers note that the government would push hard for more flexibility on EU fiscal targets and, in a more extreme scenario, breach the rules outright, reviving bond market volatility. On migration, Italy could refuse to take back asylum seekers from other member states under the EU’s Dublin rules, undermining implementation of the bloc’s migration pact.

Industry observers note that in considering these elections together, it becomes clear that the danger facing the EU is not that the union will suddenly collapse but that the political consensus that underpins European integration could begin to unravel in its key member states. The risks are not all equal. A Le Pen presidency is the most likely and most consequential for the EU, while political paralysis in Germany also looks increasingly difficult to avoid. Although Poland’s elections could produce a moderate center-right government, a far-right government or a period of protracted instability now looks increasingly plausible. Italy’s trajectory is perhaps the least threatening, but a government dependent on Vannacci would create another impediment to broader European cooperation.

Industry observers note that nor do all four races need to deliver the worst-case scenarios for the consequences in the EU to be far-reaching. A Le Pen victory in France combined with paralysis in Germany would itself throw up major problems for the EU, including a possible bond market crisis in France that could infect the broader eurozone. If Poland and Italy also moved in that direction, the EU could find itself without a functioning coalition of major states willing and able to address the growing security and economic challenges the continent is facing.

Recent findings suggest that the biggest victim of these looming changes is likely Ukraine and, by extension, Europe’s own security. The burden of supporting Ukraine financially would fall on a smaller group of member states in northwestern Europe, but they by themselves would not be able to fully compensate for the loss of support from the likes of France and Germany.

The EU has survived previous internal and external crises because its major powers ultimately judged that their interests were better served by collaboration and integration than by going their own way. The danger in 2027 is that this election supercycle will deliver outcomes that mean this assumption no longer holds. Even if the EU perseveres through the upheaval ahead, it could lose something much more profound: the underlying political consensus that has allowed the bloc to function since its creation, seven decades ago. That would not be the formal end of the European project. But it could mark the beginning of its irreversible decline.

Loudoun County parent Rachel Pisani joins 'Fox & Friends' to express outrage over school lesson aims teaching children that Thanksgiving is a 'Day of Mourning.' Pisani argues the 'woke' curriculum teaches children to hate their country.

Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

It has been revealed that on Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm.".

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

Recent findings suggest that at the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving.".

TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN ‘MISSES CORE IDEOLOGY' AND MUST TARGET LINGERING DANGER ON CAMPUSES, WATCHDOG WARNS.

A modern recreation of the first Thanksgiving in the autumn of 1621 at Plimoth Patuxet Museums (formerly Plimoth Plantation) in Plymouth, Mass. (Courtesy of Kathy Tarantola/Plimoth Patuxet Museums).

Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

Recent findings suggest that "The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek.".

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which noted the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes.".

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving.".

George Washington University hosted an event on Nov. 18 called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration." (iStock).

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson looks teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning.".

On its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities.".

In a recent development, oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.
